sections.title: Relative clauses, wh-phrase omission and relative that
texts: A relative clause modifies a noun group, often by identifying which person or thing is meant. A noun complement can supply the content of a report, claim, or similar noun.
I read the report [that the pier had closed]. I read the report [that Vic filed [•]].

Ask what the clause tells you about the report. “That the pier had closed” supplies the report’s content. It is a noun-complement clause and attaches beside N. In “that Vic filed”, the clause identifies the report and “filed” has a gap in its object position. That makes it a relative clause attached beside NOM.

Use the pro-form “one” from Chapter 7 as a second clue. “I read the one that Vic filed” keeps the relative clause outside the NOM replaced by “one”. In the content reading, the clause belongs inside the NOM that the pro-form replaces. Check which reading your substitution actually preserves.

The object relative works without an overt wh-expression. Its object gap still supplies what Vic carried and links back to lantern. Compare “the lantern which fell”, where which corresponds to the subject. Dropping which from that subject relative does not preserve the structure.

Omission also fails when more material has moved with the wh-word: “the guide with whom Rae travelled” cannot become “the guide with Rae travelled”. It can become “the guide Rae travelled with” because with stays in the lower clause. In “the family whose house Rae rented”, whose cannot simply disappear from the fronted NP.
The lamp [that Vic fixed [•]] glowed. The news [that Vic fixed the lamp] spread.
In the main analysis for this chapter, relative that fills C2, in the same place as which. The object position after fixed is a gap linked to lamp.

A separate analysis puts that in C1 and leaves the higher wh-expression covert. The diagrams here use the C2 analysis consistently. In the news example, that introduces a content clause with an overt object the lamp and no relative wh-chain.
A noun complement tells what a noun such as “claim” contains. A relative clause modifies a nominal or noun phrase. Ask whether the clause tells what the claim says or which claim the speaker means.
The complete clause “the ferry was late” gives the claim’s content. S′ attaches beside N.

You can leave out the wh-word in this object relative. Compare the subject relative in “The guide who waved wore a hat”. “Who” is the subject of “waved”. Leaving it out gives “The guide waved wore a hat” and breaks the relative-clause reading.

sections.title: Restrictive and non-restrictive relative clauses
texts: A restrictive relative helps identify which people or things are meant. A non-restrictive relative comments on a group that the reader can already identify.
The runners [who trained indoors] finished first. The runners, [who trained indoors], finished first.

Imagine a race with runners who trained in different places. “The runners who trained indoors finished first” narrows the group to the indoor runners. The restrictive relative attaches to NOM. The determiner “the” therefore applies to the group described by “runners who trained indoors”.

Now suppose the speakers already know which runners are meant. “The runners, who trained indoors, finished first” makes a claim about that whole group and adds the training location as a separate comment. This non-restrictive relative attaches to the full NP. Commas help show the comment in writing. In this pattern, use an overt wh-expression such as “who” for a non-restrictive relative.
A restrictive relative tells which members of a group are meant. A non-restrictive relative adds a detail about a group you can already identify. Check what each statement says was removed.

Picture two sets of lanterns, some cracked and some intact. A restrictive relative can identify the cracked ones. If everyone already knows which lanterns are meant, the clause can instead add that they had cracked. The tree places that second kind of comment beside the complete NP.
The lanterns [which had cracked] were removed.
The lanterns, [which had cracked], were removed.
The relative joins “lanterns” under a larger NOM. “The” determines the whole group “lanterns which had cracked”.

sections.title: Part I: Infinitives and participles
texts: A bare infinitive uses the base form of the verb without infinitival “to”. The tree can mark the verb with [-tense].
They [open the gate] daily. Rae made [them open the gate].

The first “open” heads a finite predicate. Change the time to yesterday and you can use “opened”. In “Rae made them open the gate”, the lower “open” stays in the stem form. The higher verb “made” carries the tense. The clause “[them open the gate]” contains the lower subject and its untensed VP.

This is a bare infinitive because the lower lexical verb is a stem without the infinitival marker “to” or a preceding auxiliary in that VP. The feature [-tense] distinguishes it from a present-tense form with the same spelling. A bare infinitive can also follow the copula in “All Rae did was loosen the hinge”.
Rae hopes [to have finished by noon]. The hull seems [to be being painted].

In “to have finished”, the infinitival marker “to” is analysed as an untensed auxiliary and bears [-tense]. It selects the plain stem “have”. That perfect auxiliary then selects the participle “finished”. In a shorter infinitive such as “to finish”, “to” selects the lexical stem directly.

Read “to be being painted” the same way. The first “be” is progressive and selects “being”. The second “be” is passive and selects “painted”. The chain can use perfect, progressive and passive forms in their usual order. A modal such as “can” is finite and does not fit after infinitival “to”.
[The parcel sealed], the crew took a break. [Sealed in wax], the parcel stayed dry.

A passive participial clause can consist of a lexical verb in the passive participle form without an overt passive “be”. In “the parcel sealed”, “sealed” is [-tense] and the parcel is the overt subject of the lower clause. The parcel is also what someone sealed, so the tree marks an object gap after V.

In “Sealed in wax, the parcel stayed dry”, the participial clause has no overt subject of its own. The main clause subject supplies that interpretation. Keep the two empty positions apart: the covert subject is understood from “the parcel”, and the passive object gap marks what was sealed.
[Knowing the route], Mina took the lead. Mina was [reading the map].
Knowing heads an untensed -ing clause with no progressive auxiliary. It expresses a state.

An auxiliary can also bear -ing directly, as in “Having locked the gate, Mina left”. Having is untensed PERF, and locked is the participle it selects. In the second sentence, tensed progressive was takes a VP beginning with reading. The same ending appears in both environments, so check the entire construction.

Infinitives and participles are forms that lack tense. Read [-tense] as “minus tense”. In the trees on this page, it marks the untensed verb or auxiliary. See which branch has that mark in each example.
“Wait” is a bare infinitive. It uses the plain verb form without “to”. Put [-tense] on V.
In a to-infinitive, put [-tense] on the branch above “to”. The verb “inspect” stays in its plain form.
“Packed” is a passive participle. Put [-tense] on V. “The lamps” is the subject of the passive clause, even though the lamps are what someone packed. The object spot is empty.
“The lamps” is the overt subject. It carries index 1.

texts: A to-infinitive uses “to” followed by a verb in its base form. In the inspection tree below, “to” bears [-tense] and sits beside the lexical VP “inspect the bridge”.

Inside the smaller VP, “to” bears [-tense] and takes “inspect the bridge” as its VP complement. In that lowest VP, “the bridge” belongs with “inspect”.

sections.title: Non-finite complementisers and fronted wh-phrases (C1 and C2)
texts: [For Rae to leave now] would be risky. Vic wondered [whether to leave].

In “For Rae to leave now would be risky”, “for” fills C1 and introduces a to-infinitival clause with the overt subject “Rae”. In “Vic wondered whether to leave”, “whether” fills C1 and introduces a yes/no choice. The person who would leave is supplied by the higher subject, Vic.

An overt subject does not always mean “for” can be added. In “Vic expected Rae to leave”, “Rae” is overt and C1 is empty. Alongside “Vic waited for Rae”, ask whether “for” introduces a to-infinitival clause or heads a PP whose NP complement is “Rae”. Its category depends on that structure.
Vic asked [which route to take [•]]. Vic found a route [to take [•]].

In “Vic asked which route to take”, “which route” is an overt wh-expression in C2. It corresponds to the object gap after “take”. “Vic” helps identify who is understood to take the route. C2 and the unspoken subject do different jobs.

In “Vic found a route to take”, the clause modifies the nominal “route”. The wh-expression in C2 is covert and is linked both to “route” and to the object gap. The person who takes the route still occupies a separate, unspoken subject position. In a tree, trace each link before applying an index.

An overt subject has words you can point to. A covert subject is understood without words. It can mean people in general. Then it is free. If a word group in the larger clause tells who it is, that group is its controller.
[Knowing the route] helps. · Nia enjoys [checking the maps]. · Nia enjoys [Ivo checking the maps].
The dot marks a free subject. The example makes a general statement about knowing the route.

A complementiser can start the clause. “For” fills C1 before a spoken subject. In the next example, “whether” fills C1 and the subject is silent. In the example with “what”, C2 is filled and C1 is empty.

Compare “for Ivo to wait” and “whether to wait”. In the first, C1 is “for” and “Ivo” is the spoken subject of “wait”. In the second, C1 is “whether”, and the subject may have to be inferred from the larger sentence. In “Nia knew what to pack”, “what” belongs in C2 and points to an object gap after “pack”. That object gap is separate from the understood subject, Nia.
[For Ivo to wait outside] seemed unfair. · Nia wondered [whether to wait]. · Nia knew [what to pack].

sections.title: Part II: Non-finite subjects, adjective and preposition complements, and adverbials
texts: [For Inez to leave early] would help. It would help [for Inez to leave early].

The infinitival clause supplies what would help. It can be initial or follow an expletive it in this sentence. An -ing clause can also be an initial subject, as in “Leaving early would help”. Which forms extrapose naturally depends on the construction.

Compare “Repainting the hall would be a nuisance” with “It would be a nuisance repainting the hall”. An -ing clause with an overt subject resists this shift in the book’s example pattern: “Vic repainting the hall would amuse us” does not give the same construction if moved after “It would amuse us”.
Inez was [eager to move]. The piano was [hard to move].

In the first, Inez is understood as the subject of move. In the second, the piano is understood as its object, and someone else does the moving. “It was hard to move” can use referring it for an object such as a piano. In “It was hard to move the piano”, the clause supplies what was hard and it is expletive.

On is the head of the PP. The -ing clause is its complement. The book treats -ing as the non-finite form that can follow a preposition in this role. The whole PP is selected by insisted. Contrast an optional purpose clause after a complete VP, as in “Inez stopped to check the gate”.

Separate the job of the PP from the job of the clause inside it. In “Inez insisted on checking the gate”, “checking the gate” fills the slot after “on”, and the whole PP completes “insisted”. In “Inez left after checking the gate”, the same kind of clause still completes P, but the whole PP gives the time of leaving.
Rae walked back [to check the lock]. [Hearing the bell], Rae stopped.

The to-clause gives a purpose. The -ing clause gives circumstances of the stopping. Rae supplies the understood subject of each. A non-finite adverbial can also have an overt subject, as in “The gates being locked, Rae headed home”. Some keep a subordinating conjunction in C1, as in “Rae will help if needed” or “Keep the clay covered unless using it”.
Find the subject and verb first. Then ask what job the whole clause does in the sentence.
The bracketed clause tells what takes time. It is the subject.
The clause completes the preposition “on”. That makes it the complement of P inside the PP. Here, P takes S directly.

The clause tells why someone paused. It works as an adverbial of purpose. An adjective can also select a non-finite clause, as “eager” does in “eager to help”. Next, compare the two ways a non-finite clause can belong to an NP.

sections.title: Non-finite noun complements and NOM modifiers
texts: A promise has content. In “the promise to check the lock”, the clause tells what was promised, so the whole infinitive is a complement of N within NP. “A decision to wait” and “a request for Rae to call” work similarly. The noun selects content, which can be expressed with an overt or a covert subject depending on the pattern.

Compare “a request to move the crates” with “the crates to move”. The first clause gives the content of a request and includes the object “the crates”. The second helps specify which crates, and “move” has an object gap. Use that gap and the meaning of the clause to distinguish a noun complement from a NOM modifier.
The book [to borrow] is here. The child [carrying it] waved. The book [borrowed last week] is here.

Each bracketed group modifies a NOM restrictively in this analysis. Read “to borrow” with an object gap and a covert wh-expression linked to book. In the -ing relative, the child is understood as carrying. In the passive-participial relative, book is what was borrowed.

Track the relative link and any additional passive gap separately. In “the parcel wrapped in blue paper”, link the NOM parcel to covert C2 and to the subject gap it leaves. That subject corresponds to a lower object gap after wrapped in the passive. In “a map to follow”, the map instead links to the object gap after follow, and a different, unspoken person follows it.

Ask what the clause tells you about the noun. In “a request to move the crates”, it gives the request’s content. In “the crates to move”, it tells which crates, and there is an object gap after “move”.

Try the question “What did the request ask for?” The answer is “to move the crates”, which gives the request’s content. For “the crates to move”, ask “Which crates?” The relative identifies them, and “move” leaves the object unspoken. The guide follows that gap back to the nominal “crates”.
“To move the crates” is the content of the request. It joins N within NOM.

sections.title: Non-finite verb complements and Type I and Type II verbs
texts: Rae [believed Vic to be ready]. Rae [watched Vic working]. Rae [said that Vic was ready].

Believe, watch and say can all take NP objects in some uses. Their clause patterns differ. Believe allows the to-clause in the example, while watch allows an -ing clause or a bare infinitive and say allows a finite that-clause. Wonder selects a question, as in “Rae wondered whether to leave”.
The six labels from Chapter 4 cannot capture these differences by themselves.

Compare “Rae remembered to lock the gate” with “Rae remembered locking the gate”. The first says Rae remembered and did the task. The second describes Rae’s memory of something already done. In this analysis a non-finite clause selected by V can be shown simply as a V complement without wrapping it in NP.
Type I and Type II verbs differ in where the noun phrase goes. The labels V(I) and V(II) mark the two patterns in the worked trees.
Rae expected [Vic to leave]. Rae persuaded Vic [• to leave].

Expected takes one clause complement with Vic as the overt subject. Persuaded takes the direct object Vic and a separate clause, whose covert subject Vic controls. In “Rae expected there to be a delay”, expletive there can fill the embedded subject slot. It cannot be the person persuaded.

The form him or them does not settle this choice: the book allows an object-form overt subject in certain non-finite clauses, as in “Them leaving so early surprised us”. The fact that the same person leaves in both examples also fits both structures. Some verbs select a clause without an overt subject, as in “Rae hopes to leave”. With “Rae promised Vic to leave”, the higher subject Rae controls the leaving.

With a Type I verb, labelled V(I), the non-finite clause is one complement with its own subject. With a Type II verb, labelled V(II), the higher verb takes an object and a separate non-finite clause. In the examples below, “expect” is Type I. It takes one clause with its own overt subject. “Persuade” is Type II here. It takes an object and a clause with a covert subject.
The clause is the single complement of V(I). Ivo is its overt subject.

sections.title: Finite rules for infinite languages
texts: Recursion lets a rule apply within its own result. This makes it possible to describe structures with more layers using the same finite set of rules.
The lamp stood by the box [that held the map [that showed the trail]].

Start with a sentence the language already allows. A rule such as S → S and S can join it to another sentence to make a new S. You can feed that new S into the rule again. The number of rules stays fixed, while the sentence can keep growing.

Relative clauses can grow the same way. In the example, “that held the map” contains “the map that showed the trail”. Another relative could describe the trail. A flat description can list the coordinated clauses at one level. A repeated binary rule shows what was joined at each step. A grammar can use such a small rule system to describe an unbounded set of possible sentences.
A derivation shows the steps that build a structure. Join the first two sentences. Then follow that whole group into the next step.

Use the rule S → S and S as a recipe. “Iris rests” and “Leo waits” each already count as S, so they can be the two inputs. The result “Iris rests and Leo waits” also counts as S. You can feed that entire result into the next rule application alongside “Mina waves”.
The rule joins “Iris rests” and “Leo waits”. The result is an S.
The tree shows one way to build the sentence. You can get the same words in the same order by joining “Leo waits” and “Mina waves” first.

sections.title: Grammars and sentence analysis
texts: Toy grammar: S → NP VP. NP → Rae or Vic. VP → sings or reads.

These three instructions generate sentences such as Rae reads and Vic sings. They also show how the words combine. Speakers often know whether a pattern works without reciting rules. An analyst makes that knowledge explicit by testing rules against examples. The idea of modeling a speaker’s internal knowledge comes from the generative tradition associated with Noam Chomsky. Explicit rules can reveal an assumption that was hidden in an earlier description.
Use “Rae sings”, “Vic reads”, and the rule S → S and S.

Derive “Rae sings and Vic reads and Rae sings” with either a left or right grouping. Each groups three clauses but starts from different inputs. If a proposed rule instead allows and between any two words, it would wrongly accept “Rae and reads” in this toy grammar. The written synthesis should explain both membership and grouping.

When two derivations create the same words in the same order, bracket the first join to make the difference visible. For example, one derivation first joins “Rae sings” with “Vic reads”. The other first joins “Vic reads” with the last “Rae sings”. A derivation records when a group was formed, while the final tree shows where that group ended up.
A phrase marker shows the groups in a string of words. A rule says which groups can go together and which goes first. Try this with a second small grammar.

Keep two questions separate. First, can the grammar build the string? Second, what grouping does the derivation give the string? A tree answers the grouping question for a particular derivation. The rules give you a way to check any new string against the toy grammar.
Here DET can be “the”, N can be “dog”, and V can be “waits”. The first rule places NP before VP.

The first line follows the rule. “The dog” is NP and “waits” is VP, so NP comes first. The second line puts VP first, so this toy grammar has no derivation for it. You can still put brackets around both groups. The rule explains why their order matters.
